Today he'd brought his latest piece: a black and white photograph of the pier at sunset, printed on expensive matte paper. He wanted to color it, then offer signed copies online for thirty-five dollars each. The math seemed straightforward enough. He remember reading somewhere that you needed to mark things up from cost, so thirty-five dollars seemed reasonable for the work involved.

The employee, a woman with paint-stained fingers, examined his print. "You're going to hand-color these?" Max nodded. She set it down carefully. "You know these pencils you'd use—the professional ones—those aren't cheap, right? Each print, you're probably looking at two or three dollars in supplies if you want them to look good. Max hadn't calculated his time at all. He'd thought of it as a hobby, not labor. "I mean, I'd be doing it anyway," he said.

"Sure, but if you're selling it, that's different." She leaned against the counter. "How many hours per print?"

He thought about his last piece, how the coloring had taken him six hours across three evenings. "Maybe six?"

"And you're selling them for thirty-five?"

The question hung there. Max pulled out his phone and did the math while she watched. Supplies were about eight dollars per print. Six hours of work at even minimum wage was forty-five dollars. That meant he'd need to charge at least sixty dollars per print just to break even on his time, and that wasn't even profit—that was just covering what he actually spent.

"Yeah," she said, not unkindly. "People don't always think about what things actually cost to make."

He left the store without buying anything, walking to the bus stop with his notebook still in hand. The Instagram comments about his prints suddenly felt different. The special thing about his work, he realized, wasn't special enough to command a price that reflected the reality of making it.

She'd been working toward this for months, but lately the drawings felt thin, like she was tracing someone else's vision. She'd started following this artist on Instagram—someone whose work was clean and digital and somehow captured exactly what Lea was trying to say, but better. So she'd begun studying each post, taking screenshots, even tracing some of the compositions onto her own work. Not copying, exactly. Learning, she'd told herself. But three weeks ago, she'd noticed something. The artist had only been active for six months, yet had tens of thousands of followers. Lea had clicked deeper and found an interview where the artist mentioned using an AI tool that could generate visual concepts from text descriptions. The artist didn't hide it—they described the process openly, almost boastfully. Lea felt something collapse inside her when she read it. She'd been studying work that was half-algorithm, half-person, and now she couldn't unsee it.

She'd tried to explain this to her friend Marcus at lunch. "So they're cheating?" he'd asked, mouth full of sandwich. "Not really," Lea had said slowly. "They're just using a tool." "Same thing," Marcus had said. But she didn't think it was the same. What bothered her wasn't that the artist had used the tool—it was that she couldn't tell which parts came from them and which came from the machine. There was no way to know where the person ended and the algorithm began.

Now, at the library table, Lea pulled up the artist's latest post. She studied the brushwork, the color theory, the composition. All excellent. But knowing what she knew now, she couldn't appreciate it the way she had before. It was like finding out a magic trick used mirrors. The trick was still impressive, technically, but something had changed in how she experienced it.

She turned back to her own sketchbook. The drawing she'd been working on—the one she'd partially based on one of the artist's concepts—suddenly looked like a confession. She could see the influence now, or the imitation, or whatever it was. "Mom?" Lily set down her own bag and pulled up a chair. "Are you okay?"

Her mother startled, then smiled—the careful kind. "Just reviewing some numbers before a meeting. Nothing to worry about." But she didn't put the phone away, and Lily could see the muscle in her jaw working. The document was titled "Supply Chain Analysis Q4."

Lily had come to the library to work on her college applications, but instead she sat with her mother for twenty minutes, watching her toggle between the spreadsheet and what seemed to be news articles about shipping delays and port congestion in Southeast Asia. When her mother finally had to leave for work, Lily asked, "Is something happening with your company?"

"We source textiles from Bangladesh," her mother said, gathering her things. "The factories there are having trouble getting materials in because of port issues thousands of miles away. It's creating this domino effect. Costs are going up, delivery dates are slipping, and now we're liable for penalties if we can't meet our contracts with retailers." She paused at the library door. "It's not just us, either. Apparently dozens of companies are dealing with this."

After she left, Lily tried to focus on her essays, but she found herself picking up her phone instead, searching "Bangladesh textile industry" and "global supply chains." What she learned was that most of the world's clothing comes from a handful of countries, and when something goes wrong in one place—a port closes, a ship gets stuck, a factory floods—the consequence ripples everywhere. A delay in Vietnam meant a shortage in Toronto. A strike in Malaysia affected prices in stores her mother shopped at.

She sat back, struck by something she hadn't quite considered before. The cheap sweater she'd bought last month, the one that cost thirteen dollars, existed only because of this vast, invisible web of decisions and dependencies and risks that spanned continents. Her mother's stress wasn't isolated either. It connected to factory workers who might lose hours if orders were cancelled, to retailers who'd mark items down to clear inventory, to logistics companies hiring frantically to manage the backlog, to the fuel burned by ships waiting in queue.

Over the next week, Lily mentioned none of this to her mother directly. Instead, she began noticing things differently. At the mall with friends, she lingered in clothing stores, reading labels, imagining the route each garment had taken. She looked at her mother's face during dinner on Friday, noting how she relaxed slightly after a phone call, how she'd been carrying tension in her shoulders for days. One evening, Lily overheard her talking to a colleague about diversifying their supplier base—spreading orders across more countries so that a crisis in one wouldn't devastate everything.

"It's more expensive upfront," her mother was saying. "But the alternative is... well, we're not stable as we are."

Lily realized then that her mother wasn't just managing a business problem. She was caught between competing demands: the pressure to keep costs low enough to stay competitive, the need to pay workers fairly, the responsibility to be reliable to retailers and to the people who bought the clothes, and the imperative to protect herself and her employees from shocks that were increasingly beyond anyone's control. "It is," her mother said.

Her mother considered this. "Theoretically. Though it also means fewer orders for each factory, which means fewer jobs in some places. There's no right answer. It's all consequences." She reached across the table and squeezed Lily's hand. "I'm glad you're thinking about these things."
